DNA polymerase has two important restrictions: it is able to add nucleotides only in the 5' to 3' direction (a new DNA

strand can be only extended in this direction). It also requires a free 3'-OH group to which it can add nucleotides by forming a phosphodiester bond between the 3'-OH end and the 5' phosphate of the next nucleotide. This essentially means that it cannot add nucleotides if a free 3'-OH group is not available. Then how does it add the first nucleotide? The problem is solved with the help of a primer that provides the free 3'-OH end. Another enzyme, RNA primase, synthesizes an RNA segment that is about five to ten nucleotides long and complementary to the template DNA. Because this sequence primes the DNA synthesis, it is appropriately called the primer. DNA polymerase can now extend this RNA primer, adding nucleotides one-by-one that are complementary to the template strand (Figure 14.14). response.answer_text: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction, and it needs a free 3'-OH group to extend from [ev_006]. Because the two template strands are antiparallel, one new strand can be extended continuously toward the replication fork; this is the leading strand [ev_001] [ev_007]. The other new strand is synthesized away from the replication fork in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, and each fragment needs its own RNA primer to start synthesis; this is the lagging strand [ev_001] [ev_007]. The overall direction of the lagging strand is 3' to 5', and that of the leading strand is 5' to 3' [ev_002]. RNA primers are replaced by DNA as synthesis proceeds: DNA pol I removes the primers by its exonuclease activity, uses the DNA behind the RNA as its own primer, and fills the gaps with DNA nucleotides [ev_002]. Because the two template strands are antiparallel, one new strand can be extended continuously toward the replication fork; this is the leading strand [1] [4]. The other new strand is synthesized away from the replication fork in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, and each fragment needs its own RNA primer to start synthesis; this is the lagging strand [1] [4]. The overall direction of the lagging strand is 3' to 5', and that of the leading strand is 5' to 3' [2]. RNA primers are replaced by DNA as synthesis proceeds: DNA pol I removes the primers by its exonuclease activity, uses the DNA behind the RNA as its own primer, and fills the gaps with DNA nucleotides [2]. The remaining nicks between the newly synthesized DNA and the previously synthesized DNA are sealed by DNA ligase, which forms phosphodiester linkages between the 3'-OH end of one nucleotide and the 5' phosphate end of the adjoining fragment [2].
